identification.summary: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 tracks this China-nexus espionage actor as CL-STA-0043, later TGR-STA-0043, and in September 2025 named it Phantom Taurus [S1][S4]. Unit 42 says it targets government and telecommunications organizations in Africa, the Middle East and Asia, with a focus on ministries of foreign affairs, embassies, geopolitical events and military operations [S1][S5]. Its recent toolset is the NET-STAR fileless .NET suite for IIS servers [S4][S6].
identification.firstObserved: Unit 42 first documented the cluster as CL-STA-0043 on June 2023 [S3]. Coverage of the Operation Diplomatic Specter report says activity dates to at least late 2022 [S8]. Coverage of the 2025 report describes about two and a half years of observed activity [S4].
identification.notes: Name history per Unit 42 coverage: CL-STA-0043 (2023), TGR-STA-0043 (2024, Operation Diplomatic Specter), Phantom Taurus (2025) [S3][S8][S4]. Unit 42 links CL-STA-0043 to a separate cluster, CL-STA-0002, through a shared credential-theft technique (Ntospy/NPPSpy) but says the two are distinct [S8]. Unit 42's own pages could not be fetched in this session; Unit 42 content is taken from search-result excerpts and secondary coverage. Reporting spells the NET-STAR backdoor inconsistently (IIServerCore vs ISServerCore) [S6].

attribution.sponsor: Unit 42 assesses Phantom Taurus as a Chinese state-aligned (China-nexus) espionage actor [S1][S4]. No government attribution or named PRC organization was found in the sources gathered.
attribution.confidence: Vendor assessment by Unit 42 only. Coverage of the 2024 report says Unit 42 assessed TGR-STA-0043 as a single actor working for Chinese state-aligned interests, with anecdotal evidence of ties to Beijing [S8].
attribution.basis: Coverage of the 2024 Unit 42 report cites infrastructure overlapping with other China-aligned campaigns and targeting of politicians, military personnel, foreign ministries and embassies, with anecdotal evidence of ties to Beijing; tools and infrastructure are shared across groups, so attribution remains uncertain [S8]. CyberScoop-based coverage also mentions shared infrastructure and tactics with BackdoorDiplomacy [S5].

objectives: Collection of sensitive, non-public geopolitical, diplomatic and military intelligence from government and telecommunications targets, including email and database contents [S1][S4][S5].

sectors: Government (ministries of foreign affairs, embassies, diplomatic and economic missions, military operations)
targeting.notes: CyberScoop reports Unit 42 did not name victims and that the group hit almost ten victims of geopolitical importance [S5]. Coverage of the 2024 report gives differing victim counts (at least seven vs at least nine governments) [S8]. Unit 42 states a focus on foreign affairs ministries, embassies, geopolitical events and military operations [S1].

capabilities.summary: Early activity (2023) used credential theft with Mimikatz and ntdsutil NTDS.dit dumping, and a novel use of a malicious network provider DLL (ntos.dll) registered by PowerShell, a technique previously seen only as a proof of concept [S3]. The 2024 reporting describes Exchange server email exfiltration, ProxyShell and ProxyLogon exploitation, and Gh0st RAT variants named TunnelSpecter and SweetSpecter [S8]. In 2025 Unit 42 reported a shift from email theft toward direct attacks on databases and internet-facing IIS servers, including a script run via WMI that queries SQL Server and exports results to CSV [S6]. The NET-STAR suite is a fileless .NET toolset comprising the IIServerCore backdoor and AssemblyExecuter V1 and V2 loaders, with AMSI and ETW bypasses and time-stomping reported [S4][S6]. Other tools reported: China Chopper, Potato suite, Impacket, Specter and Ntospy [S7].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing Exchange and IIS servers, and the SQL databases behind them, are key terrain for government and telecom networks [S6][S8]. STEP 2: The actor's infrastructure overlaps with other China-aligned campaigns, complicating infrastructure-based attribution [S8]. STEP 3: Template is Exchange or IIS exploitation, credential theft, then email or database collection, with fileless in-memory implants evading disk and AMSI/ETW detection [S3][S4][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued diplomatic and military intelligence collection against foreign ministries and telecoms in the Middle East, Africa and Asia [S1]. MDCOA is extension of database-focused collection to defense or coalition partner networks hosted on IIS during a regional crisis. Candidate indicators: unexpected IIS modules or in-memory .NET assemblies, new network provider registry entries (ntos), WMI-launched SQL export scripts, anomalous Exchange mailbox exports [S3][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track partner-nation foreign ministry and telecom compromises as indicators of exposure for coalition communications. (2) Authorities: server-side hunt and remediation on partner or contractor networks requires coordination with network owners and DC3. (3) Mission assurance: harden and monitor Exchange, IIS and SQL servers; enable logging that exposes in-memory .NET activity. (4) Coordination: share indicators through vendor-to-government channels, noting that attribution rests on one vendor's assessment [S1].

provenance.importedSummary: CL-STA-0043 is a Chinese state-nexus cyber-espionage actor tracked by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, which promoted the activity cluster to the named threat actor Phantom Taurus in September 2025, having previously designated it TGR-STA-0043 and linked it to the Operation Diplomatic Specter campaign. The group targets government and telecommunications organizations, including ministries of foreign affairs, embassies and diplomatic missions, across Africa, the Middle East and Asia, with a focus on geopolitical and military intelligence collection. It typically gains access by exploiting internet-facing Internet Information Services (IIS) and Microsoft Exchange servers, then performs reconnaissance and privilege escalation using native Windows tooling. In more recent operations the actor deployed NET-STAR, a fileless .NET malware suite targeting IIS web servers that comprises the IIServerCore backdoor and the AssemblyExecuter V1 and V2 loaders.
